title: Animal Behavior
description: Ten essays, reports and profiles about how animals think and act: puzzle-solving crows, head-tilting dogs, migrating cranes, dancing bees, octopuses, elephants, playful young animals, a wolf biologist in Yellowstone, peacemaking chimpanzees and a bingo night for a bird rescue center.

lessons.title: The Crow and the Riddle
lessons.summary: A column explains how crows and their relatives make tools, solve puzzles and hide their food from thieves.
lessons.text:
There is an old saying that insanity is doing the same thing over and over and expecting a different result. If that is true, crows are in no danger of insanity. Give a crow a riddle, and it will rarely repeat an unsuccessful move for long. When one attempt is unsuccessful, it tries something else.

Crows and ravens have long impressed people. In the myths of northern Europe, Odin, the most powerful deity of the old religion, kept two ravens called Thought and Memory, who flew around the world each day and brought him news. A deity who trusted birds with his information was making a sensible choice.

Consider the crows of New Caledonia, a group of islands in the Pacific. These birds wield tools in the wild. A crow picks a small branch, strips off the leaves and shapes the end into a tiny hook. It then wields the hook to pull insects out of holes in dead wood. Each bird seems to customize its tool for the job: a longer hook for a deep hole, a shorter one for a shallow crack. In a laboratory, one crow even customized a straight piece of wire, bending it into a hook to lift a small bucket of food out of a tube.

Researchers have also borrowed a riddle from an ancient story about a thirsty crow that drops stones into a jar until the water rises high enough to drink. In the modern test, a piece of food floats on water in a narrow tube, out of the bird's reach. Many crows soon begin dropping stones into the tube, and they prefer heavy stones that sink to light objects that float. It is hard not to call this behavior intentional: the bird seems to understand what it wants and how the stones will bring the food closer.

Some crows are stumped at first, and a stumped bird may stare at a puzzle for minutes before trying again. Yet one crow, filmed for television, solved a puzzle of eight steps in the right order, although it had only ever practiced each step on its own.

Crows are clever with secrets, too. Scrub jays, cousins of the crows, hide food to eat later. If another jay is watching while a bird hides a seed, the bird often returns alone and moves the seed to a new, concealed spot. Remarkably, the birds most likely to do this are those that have stolen food themselves. They seem to know that a hiding place is safe only while it stays concealed from thieves.

Is it feasible to compare such abilities with our own? A crow's brain is built very differently from ours, yet it has proved feasible to give crows and children the same water test, and crows do about as well as children of five to seven.

Questions:
How do the crows of New Caledonia wield tools in the wild?
They shape small branches into hooks and wield them to pull insects out of holes in dead wood.
What riddle did researchers borrow from an ancient story?
They put food on water in a narrow tube, and the crows dropped stones into it until the food rose.
Why does the column call the crows' behavior intentional?
The birds seem to understand what they want and how the stones will bring the food closer.
What does a scrub jay do when another jay watches it hide food?
It often returns alone and moves the food to a new, concealed spot.

lessons.title: Why My Dog Tilts Her Head
lessons.summary: A dog owner explains what scientists have learned about why dogs tilt their heads when they hear certain words.
lessons.text:
Every morning, while I am still in my pajamas, my dog, Maisie, sits on the ottoman in the living room and waits for me to say the word "walk." When I say it, she jumps down and runs to the door. When I say a word she only half knows, such as "ball" or "bath," something else happens: she tilts her head to one side, as if the word needs a closer look.

Maisie is not alone. People have posted countless videos of dogs tilting their heads, and the best ones are reposted until they reach every corner of the internet. In one, a dog hears a sports announcer on television and tilts its head left, then right; in another, it tilts at a radio announcer. I have reposted a few myself, but I had never asked why dogs do it until a friend sent me a study from a university in Budapest.

The researchers worked with a rare group of dogs they called gifted word learners, dogs that can fetch dozens of toys by name. When an owner asked for a toy by name, these learners tilted their heads far more often than ordinary dogs did. The scientists suggested that the tilt may be linked to listening hard to something that matters, a word the dog is trying to match with a memory. Each dog also tilted its head to the same side every time, much as many of us favor one hand.

There are other explanations. One is about hearing: by changing the angle of its head, a dog may find out more exactly where a sound is coming from. Another is about seeing. A dog with a long nose may tilt its head to see our mouth and face more clearly. None of these ideas rules out the others.

What I take from all this is a little humbling. When Maisie tilts her head, she is not performing for me; she is working. A word I say without thinking may be, for her, a puzzle with a reward at the end. Trainers warn that too many commands at once can overload a dog, and I have seen Maisie overloaded: when the whole family calls her from different rooms, she simply lies down.

I have also learned not to disappoint her. If I say "walk" as a joke, she runs to the door and then looks back with an expression so hurt that I feel I have broken a promise. An insecure dog, a trainer told me, can become anxious when words stop meaning what they used to mean, so it is kind to keep them reliable.

So now, when I come downstairs in my pajamas each morning, I choose my words with care. "Breakfast" means breakfast, and "walk" means walk. And when Maisie tilts her head, I wait, because I know that downstairs, on the ottoman, a small learner is thinking.

Questions:
What does Maisie do when she hears a word she only half knows?
She tilts her head to one side.
What were the gifted word learners in the Budapest study?
They were dogs that knew the names of many toys and could fetch them by name.
How might a head tilt help a dog to see?
A dog with a long nose may tilt its head to see a person's mouth and face more clearly.
Why does the writer try not to disappoint Maisie?
An insecure dog can become anxious when words stop meaning what they used to mean.

lessons.title: A Compass in the Eye
lessons.summary: A report on the great crane gathering in Nebraska explains what scientists know about how birds sense the Earth's magnetic field.
lessons.text:
Every March, a great spectacle takes place on the plains of the United States. Along a short stretch of the Platte River in Nebraska, several hundred thousand cranes gather to rest and feed on their long journey north. At sunset they come down to the river in waves until the shallow water is covered with gray birds. The nearby towns hold a crane fest each spring, with guided walks at dawn. The fest is busy, but the spectacle itself is quiet, and for local people the cranes usher in the spring.

How do birds find their way across a continent? They learn routes from older birds and read the sun and the stars, but many also seem to sense the magnetic field of the Earth.

The first clear evidence came from robins kept in cages in Germany more than 50 years ago. At the onset of the migration season, caged robins grow anxious at night, as if compelled to fly. They hop again and again in one direction, the direction they would fly if they were free. When scientists changed the magnetic field around the cages, the birds changed direction too. It is the changing length of the days that ushers in this behavior.

But where is the compass? Scientists have three main ideas.

The first idea was that birds carry tiny magnetic iron particles in their beaks, each nanoparticle acting like the needle of a compass. Researchers did find cells rich in iron in the beaks of pigeons, but these cells belonged to the immune system and had nothing to do with direction, so this version of the idea proved flawed, although some scientists still look for magnetic nanoparticles elsewhere in the body.

A second idea involves induction. When a wire moves through a magnetic field, a small electric current appears in it, a process called induction. Some researchers think that fluid in a bird's inner ear might work in a similar way, but the evidence is still limited.

The third idea is the strangest. Certain molecules in a bird's eye may react to the Earth's field through quantum physics, so the bird might actually see the field as a faint pattern over the landscape. This is a true crossover between physics and biology, a crossover that has attracted researchers from both fields.

One experiment supports this idea. In the German city of Oldenburg, robins lost their sense of direction when they were exposed to the weak electrical noise of ordinary electronic devices. Their compass was weakened not by a storm or an injury, but by the background noise of modern life. When their huts were covered with metal screens, the birds found their way again.

We can only approximate what a bird experiences, and even our best descriptions are approximate translations from a sense we do not have. Still, standing by the Platte at sunset, it is hard not to feel that the cranes know something we have forgotten.

Questions:
What spectacle takes place on the Platte River every March?
Several hundred thousand cranes gather there to rest and feed on their journey north.
How do caged robins behave at the onset of the migration season?
They grow anxious at night, as if they are compelled to fly in one direction.
Why did the first idea about iron particles prove flawed?
The cells rich in iron belonged to the immune system and had nothing to do with direction.
What weakened the robins' compass in Oldenburg?
The weak electrical noise of ordinary electronic devices weakened it.

lessons.title: The Dance in the Dark
lessons.summary: An explanation of how honeybees use the waggle dance to share directions, choose a new home and survive the winter.
lessons.text:
Inside a hive it is almost completely dark, yet honey bees pass on detailed directions there every day, by dancing. The language of their dance was first explained by Karl von Frisch, who shared a Nobel Prize for the work in 1973.

When a worker bee finds a good patch of flowers, she flies home and performs what is called the waggle dance on the comb. She runs forward in a straight line while shaking her body from side to side, then circles back and runs the same line again. The angle of the straight run tells the other bees the direction of the flowers. If she runs straight up, the food lies toward the sun; a run tilted to the right means food to the right of the sun. The length of the run gives the distance: the longer she shakes, the farther the others must fly.

The bees that follow the dance are often newcomers, younger workers who have just begun to collect food. A newcomer stays close behind the dancer and then flies off to find the place for itself.

The dance even has dialects. Different kinds of honey bees translate distance into dancing in slightly different ways. In one experiment, researchers kept honey bees from Asia and from Europe together in the same colony, and the bees from Asia gradually learned to read the other dialect, much as children of immigrants learn a second language.

The dance is also used to choose a home. In late spring, a crowded colony may divide. The old queen leaves with thousands of workers, and this swarm settles on a branch while scouts search for a new place to live. A homeowner who finds a swarm hanging from a tree in the yard may be alarmed, but a swarm is usually calm, because the bees have no home or young to defend. A sensible homeowner calls a local beekeeper, who collects it in a box. The scouts dance for the sites they have found, and within a day or two the swarm agrees on the best one. The continuation of the colony depends on this choice.

In winter the bees gather in a tight ball and work the muscles they use for flying, which produces heat. The center of the ball stays warm, a small living furnace, even when the air outside is freezing, and bees at the cold outer edge take turns moving in toward the furnace.

In the laboratory, bees can learn to fly through a maze by following colored marks, and a bee that has solved one maze solves the next maze faster.

People depend on all of this. Each February, more than a million colonies are trucked to California to visit the almond farms there, because almond flowers need bees to carry their pollen. The sweet liquid the bees collect gives them energy, and pollen gives them protein, built from the amino acids that young bees need to grow.

Questions:
What did the bees from Asia learn in the experiment?
They gradually learned to read the other dialect of the dance.
Why should a homeowner not fear a swarm?
A swarm is usually calm, because the bees have no home or young to defend.
What does the continuation of a colony depend on?
It depends on the swarm choosing a good new home.
What does pollen give the bees?
It gives them protein, built from amino acids.

lessons.title: Eight Arms and a Mind of Their Own
lessons.summary: A look at the octopus, a solitary animal whose intelligence developed along a path completely separate from ours.
lessons.text:
Among clever animals, the octopus is the strangest, because its intelligence developed along a path completely separate from ours. The last ancestor we share with it was probably a small, worm-like creature that lived more than 500 million years ago. Everything an octopus knows, it worked out in its own way.

Begin with the body. An octopus has about 500 million nerve cells, but most of them are not in its brain. About two-thirds sit in its eight arms. Scientists describe these arms as part of the peripheral nervous system, meaning the nerves outside the central brain, but in this animal the peripheral system is unusually powerful. An arm can taste what it touches, feel its way into a crack and even grab food on its own while the brain attends to something else. It is as if each arm had a mind of its own.

The octopus is also a solitary animal. It does not live in groups, it gets no lessons from its parents, and many species live only a year or two. A solitary life without teachers makes its abilities all the more striking. In aquariums, these animals learn to open jars to reach a crab inside, and some learn to recognize individual keepers, greeting one with interest and spraying another with water.

Researchers have uncovered other surprising skills. In Indonesia, divers watched octopuses carry halves of coconut shells across the sea floor and later hide inside them, a clear case of an animal using a tool. Studies have also uncovered how the animal changes color: its skin contains thousands of tiny bags of color that it can open and close in a fraction of a second. Strangely, most species appear to be incapable of seeing color themselves, yet they match their surroundings well. How an animal incapable of seeing color manages this is still being studied.

When hiding fails, an octopus can vanish in another way. It releases a cloud of dark ink and darts off while the predator is confused. The cloud hangs in the water like smoke and then slowly begins to dissolve. Before it can dissolve completely, the animal has usually found a crack in the rocks.

In the deep sea, where light penetration is weak, many species are red. Red light does not travel far in water, and with so little penetration of light from above, a red animal looks almost black, which is hard to see in the dark.

To a crab, this animal is a real menace. To a diver, however, it is rarely menacing. Most species are shy, and a curious one may simply reach out an arm to explore a diver's hand. Some are famous escape artists. One at an aquarium in New Zealand left its tank at night, crossed the floor and slipped down a pipe into the sea. Animals that can vanish like that make keepers check the lids of their tanks twice.

Questions:
Where are most of an octopus's nerve cells?
About two-thirds of them are in its eight arms, in its peripheral nervous system.
Why are the abilities of a solitary octopus so striking?
It gets no lessons from its parents, and it often lives only a year or two.
What did divers in Indonesia see?
They saw octopuses carry halves of coconut shells and later hide inside them.
How does an octopus use ink to vanish?
It releases a cloud of ink and darts off while the predator is confused.

lessons.title: What the Elephants Remember
lessons.summary: An essay on elephant memory: a long pregnancy, a drought in Tanzania, two old friends reunited and signs of empathy.
lessons.text:
People say that an elephant never forgets. The saying is not exactly true, but it points toward something real. Elephants can live for 60 years or more, and much of what keeps a family alive is stored in the memory of its oldest female.

Memory begins early. A young elephant spends about 22 months inside its mother, the longest pregnancy of any land animal, and the brain of the fetus develops slowly over that time. Even so, much of its learning happens after birth, as it follows its family and watches.

The value of that learning became clear during a drought in Tanzania in 1993. For months the searing heat dried up rivers and pools, the drought devastated the plants that elephants eat, and many animals were on the verge of starving. Scientists noticed a pattern. The families led by older females, who had lived through a similar drought decades earlier, left the park and walked to distant places where water could still be found. Many families led by younger females stayed behind, and that year far more of their young died. The old females, it seemed, carried a map in their heads, drawn during another searing summer long ago.

How do memories last so long? In humans, a process called consolidation turns fresh experiences into lasting memories, and much of this consolidation happens during sleep. Elephants are a puzzle here, because wild elephants seem to sleep only about two hours a night, less than any other mammal studied so far. Presently, no one knows how they manage consolidation on so little sleep, and an answer may teach us about our own memory, too.

Elephants also remember one another. A famous case comes from a sanctuary in Tennessee. In 1999, an old female named Shirley arrived there, where another old female, Jenny, already lived. The two had worked together in a circus more than 20 years earlier. When they were reunited, they roared, reached for each other with their trunks through the bars and would not be separated. Once reunited, they stayed side by side for the rest of Jenny's life.

What about feelings? Scientists are careful with such questions, but some evidence points to empathy. In a study in Thailand, elephants that saw a companion in distress went to it, touched it with their trunks and made soft calls, much as a friend might put an arm around someone who is upset. Whether this is empathy in the human sense is debated, but it looks like a close relative.

There are darker memories, too. Young elephants that have lost their mothers sometimes behave in ways that resemble trauma in humans. Some researchers wonder whether elephants have anything like a flashback, the sudden, vivid return of a frightening memory, but presently there is no way to ask them. What seems clear is that, for an elephant, the past is never entirely over.

Questions:
How long does an elephant fetus grow inside its mother?
It grows for about 22 months, the longest pregnancy of any land animal.
What happened during the drought in Tanzania in 1993?
The searing heat devastated the plants, and many animals were on the verge of starving.
Why is consolidation a puzzle in elephants?
Wild elephants seem to sleep only about two hours a night, and much consolidation happens during sleep.
What did Shirley and Jenny do when they were reunited?
They roared, reached for each other with their trunks and would not be separated.
What is a flashback?
It is the sudden, vivid return of a frightening memory.

lessons.title: Why Young Animals Play
lessons.summary: An explanation of why young animals, from donkeys to gorillas and ravens, spend so much time playing.
lessons.text:
Watch a young goat in a field for a few minutes, and you may see it suddenly leap into the air, twist its body and land facing the other way, for no reason anyone can see. A young donkey does something similar: it races in circles around its mother, kicks up its back legs and races again. The young donkey has nothing to escape and nowhere to go. It is playing.

Play is surprisingly widespread. Young dogs, cats, horses, bears and monkeys all play, and so do ravens and some parrots. Young ravens have been filmed sliding down snowy roofs, flying back to the top and sliding down again. A raven may also fling a stick into the air and catch it in flight before it hits the ground, then fling it again.

Play is not free. It burns energy, and an energetic young animal that leaps and wrestles is also easier for predators to see. So why has play survived through evolution? Researchers offer several reasons. Energetic play may train the body, building strength and balance. It may prepare young animals for the unexpected, such as a fall or an attack, by giving them practice at losing control and getting it back. And in social animals, play teaches the rules of getting along.

Young gorillas show this clearly. Two young gorillas will chase and wrestle for long periods, opening their mouths in a relaxed "play face" and making a breathy sound that resembles laughter. A bigger gorilla often holds back its strength so that the game can continue, and if one partner gets too rough, the other stops. Dogs have a signal with the same purpose: the play bow, with the front legs flat on the ground and the back end in the air, which means that what follows is a game.

Even rats seem to laugh. When researchers tickled young rats gently with their hands, the rats made high chirping sounds, too high for humans to hear, and followed the hand to be tickled again.

Not everything that looks like play is play, however. A small spotted skunk that does a handstand on its front feet is not being playful; the handstand is a warning, shown just before it sprays. And a bear cub splashing in the pools below a waterfall may be playing, or it may be practicing to fish, as the adults do at the top of the waterfall. Often, it is both.

One more lesson from play matters to anyone who cares for animals. Play is often the first thing to disappear when an animal is hungry, frightened or unhealthy. A young animal that plays is usually safe, fed and well. An unhealthy one often stops playing long before it shows other signs of trouble, which is why keepers and farmers worry when the games stop.

Questions:
What does a young donkey do when it plays?
It races in circles around its mother, kicks up its back legs and races again.
What may a young raven fling into the air?
It may fling a stick into the air and catch it in flight before it hits the ground.
How do young gorillas show that they are playing?
They open their mouths in a relaxed play face and make a sound like laughter.
Why does a spotted skunk do a handstand?
The handstand is a warning, shown just before it sprays.

lessons.title: The Woman Who Watches Wolves
lessons.summary: A profile of a field biologist who has spent twelve years watching wolf packs in Yellowstone National Park.
lessons.text:
At five o'clock on a winter morning, when the temperature in the Lamar Valley of Yellowstone National Park is often below zero, Mara Lindqvist is already standing beside the road with a telescope. Her auburn hair is pushed under a wool hat, and her breath freezes on her scarf. She is looking for wolves.

Lindqvist, 41, is a field biologist, and for most of the past 12 years her office has been this valley. After college she spent three years as an unpaid volunteer, counting animal tracks for park researchers in exchange for a bed and meals. Unpaid work was the only way in, she says, so she supported herself by writing freelance articles for nature magazines. The freelance work taught her to describe what she saw in clear prose, a skill she still uses in her field notes. "Good science starts with good prose," she likes to say. "If you can't describe what happened, you didn't really see it."

By 1926, wolves had been completely removed from Yellowstone, hunted because they killed farm animals. For nearly 70 years the park had none. Bringing them back was debated for years. Lawmakers from the surrounding states argued against the plan, and some public meetings were full of inflammatory speeches on both sides. In the end, in 1995 and 1996, 31 wolves were brought from Canada and released in the park. Today, although a few lawmakers remain unhappy, the inflammatory talk has mostly cooled, and wolves are one of the main reasons visitors come.

Lindqvist studies how packs change over time. A wolf pack is a family: a breeding pair and their young of several years. Sometimes a group of males from outside pushes into a pack and replaces the breeding male. Such a takeover can change the pack's behavior and even its territory. Lindqvist once followed a takeover for three weeks, recording every meeting between the newcomers and the family.

Snow is her best ally. In winter, every footprint tells a story, and in a line of footprints she can read where a pack walked, where it rested and where it chased elk.

She is also interested in the wider effects of wolves. Some researchers argue that, by keeping elk on the move, wolves allowed young trees to grow back along the rivers, which in turn helped beavers, since beavers need those trees for food and for building. Lindqvist has measured the stumps of trees cut by beavers along one stream. She believes the wolves played a part, but she warns that nature rarely offers a neat chain of causes.

Wolves, she notes, are hard to stop. They have returned to parts of Europe, and they even live in the radioactive forests around Chernobyl in Ukraine, which people left after the accident of 1986. "If wolves can live in a radioactive zone," she says, pulling her hat down over her auburn hair, "they can certainly share a valley with tourists."

Questions:
Why did Lindqvist work as an unpaid volunteer?
Unpaid work was the only way in, and she supported herself by writing freelance articles.
What did lawmakers from the surrounding states think of the plan?
They argued against bringing the wolves back, and some meetings were full of inflammatory speeches.
What is a takeover in a wolf pack?
It is when a group of males from outside replaces the breeding male of a pack.
What can Lindqvist read in a line of footprints?
She can read where a pack walked, where it rested and where it chased elk.

lessons.title: How Chimpanzees Make Peace
lessons.summary: An essay on how chimpanzees settle their fights, with reconciliation, peacemakers and shifting alliances.
lessons.text:
Chimpanzees are not gentle animals. Life in a group of 40 or 50 apes brings constant friction over food, over mates and above all over rank. Fights break out with an almighty noise of screams and barks that carries far through the forest. Yet groups of these apes rarely fall apart, and the reason, scientists have learned, is that they are skilled at making peace.

The Dutch scientist Frans de Waal was one of the first to study this carefully, watching a large group of apes at a zoo in the Netherlands. He noticed that soon after a fight, the two opponents often approached each other, touched hands, kissed or embraced, and then sat grooming each other's fur. He called this behavior reconciliation. Reconciliation, he argued, was not a sign of weakness but a way of protecting a relationship that both animals still needed.

Political language comes easily when describing these groups. A reconciliation between two males can look like bilateral talks between two countries: a private agreement between two sides, with no one else involved. Often the peace is provisional at first, and the two keep a careful distance for a while, just as a provisional agreement between nations is tested before it becomes permanent. Like many bilateral deals, it holds as long as both sides gain from it.

Sometimes a third party steps in. Older females have been seen bringing two males together after a fight, sitting between them and then quietly moving away so that the males are left side by side. This is not quite arbitration, in which a judge decides who is right, but it is a gentle form of peacemaking. Something nearer to arbitration also occurs: a high-ranking male may step between two fighters and stop the fight without favoring his friends. In ancient Rome, a tribune was an official whose job was to protect ordinary citizens from the powerful. The high-ranking ape who keeps the strong from bullying the weak plays a similar role, a kind of tribune of the group.

Allegiance matters as well. A male who wants to rise needs allies, and the allegiance of other males, and of the females, often decides who leads. These allegiances shift. A male may support one leader for years and then switch his allegiance to a rival, which can bring a change at the top. Grooming is the currency of these friendships, and a leading male spends many hours each day grooming his supporters.

What can people learn from this? De Waal argued that peacemaking is not a recent invention of human culture but has deep roots in our evolution. The almighty scream of a fight is one part of life among these apes; the quiet reconciliation afterward is another, and just as important.

Questions:
What causes friction in a group of chimpanzees?
Food, mates and above all rank cause friction.
What did de Waal call the behavior he saw after fights?
He called it reconciliation.
Why does the essay compare reconciliation to bilateral talks?
It is a private agreement between two sides, with no one else involved.
How is the high-ranking ape like a tribune?
Like a tribune in ancient Rome, it keeps the strong from bullying the weak by stopping their fights.

lessons.title: Bingo Night for the Owls
lessons.summary: A volunteer at a wildlife rescue center describes a bingo night that raised money to repair a flight cage for injured birds.
lessons.text:
For three years I have volunteered at a small wildlife rescue center outside our town. We care for injured birds, mostly hawks and owls, and return them to the wild when they are well. This spring our largest flight cage, where birds practice flying before they are released, badly needed an overhaul. The roof leaked and the wooden frame was rotting. The overhaul would cost about $6,000, so we decided to hold a bingo night.

The police precinct downtown lent us its community room, which is used for neighborhood meetings. The captain of the precinct had once brought us an injured owl he found by the road, and he has supported us ever since.

Our bingo caller was Walter, a retired shoe salesman who volunteers with us on weekends. Forty years as a salesman had given him a strong voice and a talent for keeping a room cheerful. A good caller, he told me, reads each number slowly and clearly and never rushes the older players.

Local businesses donated prizes. An outdoor store gave us warm apparel, jackets and hats, and a print shop made apparel with a drawing of our resident owl. A local jewelry maker donated a pair of silver earrings shaped like feathers, which became the evening's top prize. The woman who won the earrings put them on at once and wore them for the rest of the night.

My job was the food table. I made sandwiches, half with mayo and half without, because people feel strongly about mayo. My friend Rosa baked a large lemon sponge cake, and the sponge cake was gone within an hour.

The real star, though, was Athena, a barred owl who cannot fly because of an old wing injury and now helps us teach visitors. Between games, I carried Athena around the room on my glove and explained a little about owl behavior. An owl's eyes are fixed in its head, so it cannot move them as we do. Instead, it turns its whole head, up to about three-quarters of a full circle. Whenever Walter called a number, Athena turned her head toward his voice, and the room laughed every time.

One guest, a young web designer, asked about our website. It was old, and its functionality was limited: people could read about us, but they could not report an injured bird or give money online. She offered to rebuild it for free and to add the functionality we needed.

At the end of the night we counted the money: $6,400, enough for the overhaul of the flight cage. Walter called the final number, the last winner shouted "Bingo!" and Athena turned her head one more time.

Questions:
Why did the rescue center hold a bingo night?
The flight cage needed an overhaul, which would cost about $6,000.
Who was the bingo caller?
Walter, a retired shoe salesman, was the caller.
What was the top prize?
The top prize was a pair of silver earrings shaped like feathers.
Why does an owl turn its whole head?
Its eyes are fixed in its head, so it cannot move them as we do.
